body.hook: Read "I'm fine" five different ways and you'll get five different meanings: happy, angry, sad, sarcastic, scared. The words stay the same; pitch, pace and tone change everything.

study.title: Same Words, New Meaning
study.question: How do pitch, pace, tone and pause change meaning?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. Pitch ladder (5 minutes): Count from 1 to 10, rising in pitch on each number, then falling. Say "Really?" with rising inflection (a question) and falling inflection (disbelief).
2. One line, many tones (10 minutes): In pairs, say "I'm fine" as: cheerful, angry, sad, sarcastic, scared, bored. The partner guesses the tone.
3. Emphasis (5 minutes): Say "I didn't take your book," stressing a different word each time. How does meaning change? ("I didn't..." = someone else did; "...your book" = I took someone else's.)
4. The power of pause (10 minutes): "I have something to tell you... ... I'm moving away." Where does the pause go? How long?
5. Mini-dialogue (15 minutes): Perform a four-line dialogue twice with two completely different interpretations: A: "You're here." B: "I said I would be." A: "You always say that." B: "This time I mean it."
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Practise a pitch ladder and inflection
Say one line in six tones
Perform a mini-dialogue two different ways
discussion: How did moving emphasis change meaning?
Where was the pause most powerful?
What were your two interpretations of the dialogue?
study.product: Perform the mini-dialogue in two contrasting interpretations and explain the vocal choices in each.

body.objective: Students will be able to perform choral speech.
successCriteria: I can speak in unison with a group
I can use solo, small-group and full-group voices for effect

body.hook: In ancient Greek theatre, a chorus of performers spoke together, commenting on the action like one giant voice. Today, choral speech still gives poems and stories a powerful, unified sound.

vocabulary.definition: A group speaking a text together.
Everyone speaking at exactly the same time.

study.title: Many Voices, One Sound
study.question: How can a group voice bring a poem to life?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. Unison warm-up (5 minutes): The group counts 1 to 10 together, matching speed and volume exactly. Then the leader conducts with hands: louder, softer, faster, slower.
2. Techniques (10 minutes): Try the line "The wind is rising, the wind is rising" as: full unison; solo then group; building (one voice, then two, then all); canon (groups start two beats apart); echo (group repeats the last word softly).
3. Arrange a poem (20 minutes): In groups of six, arrange a short public-domain poem, such as "The Wind" by Robert Louis Stevenson (1885) or "Windy Nights" by the same poet. Mark the text: S (solo), G (small group), A (all), plus where to get louder, softer, faster or pause.
4. Perform (10 minutes): Perform with one person conducting the start. Stand in a clear formation and look up from your scripts.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; poems by Robert Louis Stevenson are in the public domain.
steps: Arrange a poem with solo, group and all parts
discussion: Which technique created the most dramatic effect?
Why did you give certain lines to a solo voice?
How did the formation help your performance?
study.product: Perform a choral arrangement of a poem using at least three techniques and submit your marked-up script.

body.objective: Students will be able to present readers theatre.
successCriteria: I can perform from a script using vocal expression
I can show character through voice alone
I can work with a group to keep the story clear and lively
body.hook: Readers theatre is drama without memorizing. Performers hold scripts and bring a story to life using only voice, face and small gestures. Some radio dramas and podcast plays work the same way: the voice has to do everything.

vocabulary.definition: Performing a script by reading aloud with expression, usually without sets or memorizing.
The written text of a play.
The line or action that signals your turn.
Looking at the audience or at a point in the room to show who you are talking to.
A voice that shows a character's age, mood and personality.
Lines that tell the story to the audience.

study.title: Read It Alive
study.question: How can voice alone bring a story to life?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. Character voices (10 minutes): Read "Who's been eating my porridge?" as Father Bear, Mother Bear and Baby Bear. Then as a robot, a sports announcer and a tired grandparent. Vary pitch, pace and tone.
2. Readers theatre rules: hold scripts at chest height, never in front of your face; look up as much as possible; pick up cues quickly; use offstage focus (looking at a point above the audience) when talking to another character; stay in character while others speak.
3. Rehearse (25 minutes): Groups of five receive a short readers theatre script adapted from a public-domain fable (for example, "The Fox and the Crow" by Aesop). Assign roles including two narrators. Highlight your lines, mark pauses and emphasis, and decide each character's voice.
4. Perform (10 minutes): Perform for the class. The audience listens with eyes closed for one minute: is the story still clear?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; Aesop's fables are in the public domain.
steps: Mark your script for pauses and emphasis
Perform and test with eyes closed
discussion: How did you make each character's voice different?
Why must cues be picked up quickly?
Was the story clear with eyes closed?
What did narrators do to keep the story moving?
study.product: Perform a readers theatre script with a distinct character voice, quick cues and marked script, and explain your vocal choices.
